newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan seen keeping stable policy despite low CPI.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan seen keeping stable policy despite low CPI.

text.p: Despite low inflation in April, the central bank was unlikely to further loosen monetary policy in case it accelerated capital outflows, economists said on Monday.
Taiwan's April consumer price index rose only 0.51 percent compared to April 1996, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said.
The increase was significantly lower than an average forecast of 1.224 percent compiled from Friday's Reuters poll of Taiwan economists.

Analysts said the low inflation rate, in theory, could revive speculation that the central bank might lower banks' reserve requirements to boost the economy, a move that the bank has repeatedly said it will take at an "appropriate time."
But they said investor unease over the government's failure to check a spate of violent crime may deter the bank from such action for fear it could hasten the outflow of foreign capital.
"Amid the current political uncertainties, any looser monetary policy will simply accelerate capital outflows," said HSBC James Capel economist Stephen Wang.

Outraged by the recent murder of a famous actress's daughter, about 40 Taiwan college students marched in front of the island's cabinet building in Taipei on Monday to demand the resignation of Premier Lien Chan and a reshuffle of the cabinet.
The students had participated in a 50,000-people rally on Sunday and staged an all-night vigil in the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, both protests against the island's worsening social order.
"The best the central bank can do now is to keep its stable-to-loose money policy in its upcoming board meeting," Wang said.
The board meeting is scheduled for May 8.
Taiwan central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong on Saturday reiterated the central bank would continue its longstanding "stable-to-loose" monetary policy.
"The central bank's monetary policy will not change. It will continue to be stable-to-loose," Sheu told reporters.
Economists added that a looser money policy is not urgent for the recovering domestic economy.
"Liquidity is still quite loose at the moment, and recent indicators announced had shown that the recovery is doing not bad," said Grand Cathay Securities vice-president Terry Chen.
"It's not necessary for the central bank to consider loosening its money policy in the near term," Chen said.
Directorate director Chan Teh-song said the low inflation would benefit Taiwan's export-driven economy.
"The low inflation should increase the competitiveness of our export products," Chan told reporters.

In April, the economics ministry said Taiwan's March industrial output rose 10.01 percent year-on-year and March export orders gained 5.61 percent year-on-year. Both figures showed higher-than-expected growth.
The directorate attributed the low April inflation to declining pork prices following the outbreak of a hog epidemic.
It said the epidemic, which has decimated consumer demand in pork since it erupted in late March, caused wholesale pork prices in April to plunge by 45 percent.
